title: Diamond in the Rough
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona shares a story about their sailing adventure as a metaphor for Buddhist practice, highlighting how often we look outside ourselves for answers when the solution lies within. This experience is meant to encourage us to pay attention to our own experiences and perceptions, rather than relying on external sources or distractions. By doing so, we can discover our true nature and overcome obstacles that prevent us from understanding and practicing the Dharma, such as desire, aversion, dullness, restlessness, and doubt.

sentences.text: An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.
I've really appreciated Tim's sharing with the two realms, who's where.
So, but I don't know if I can, oh yeah, we can tell.
So we've got Wayne, Ken, Hannah, and phone number ending in 8844.
And for you all, we've got Chris, Tim, Karen, and Linda.
That's been great.
And it is great to be here in person.
So for a couple of years, I lived on a sailboat in Blaine.
This is a Contessa 26, a 26-foot boat with a spacious 96 square feet of living space.
The model of the sailboat was known for winning distance races in years when the storms had knocked out the competition, slow and steady.
It was the same model of a sailboat piloted by Tanya Abe, who left New York Harbor in 1986 at 18 years old and became the youngest person at the time to circle the world solo.
The title of this talk is Diamond in the Rough.
Speaking of diamonds, I have an error to correct.
At a talk a couple of months ago, I misattributed the sutra with the great teaching where Buddha sits down to give a Dharma talk, and he turned his attention to what was before him.
Very important teaching, which that is, I discovered in fact from the Diamond Sutra.
So I'm delighted that Hannah will be guiding us through that work during our practice period starting next month.
So I'm going to share with you one of the stories that's threaded through Tanya Abe's book about her sailing adventure, *Made in Voyage*.
She writes, *In Bermuda, my father stayed with me on Baruna, that's her sailboat, for one week.
One night when we sat down to work out the finer points in navigation, he was appalled to discover that I didn't know that two lines of position are needed for a fix.
I had been navigating all the way from New York with only one.
He was incredulous.
How?
How could you possibly locate this tiny island with your navigation completely screwed up?
I don't know, I answered.
I just homed my radio direction finder in on Bermuda.*
You just homed your...
Aye, no Tanya, face it, you made it here by pure dumb luck.
He closed his eyes and shook his head.
Tanya, listen to me carefully.
There are no RDF beacons that will help you find St.
Thomas.
You'll have to find it entirely on your own, do you understand?
Yeah, sure, I know.
But I had a lot of bad weather and hardly any time to work on my navigation.
I'll get the hang of it on the way to St.
Thomas.
He grimaced in pain, you better get the hang of it.
If you miss St.
Thomas, you'll end up in Puerto Rico.
If you miss Puerto Rico, God knows where you'll end up.
You better be sure you understand everything before you leave.
Ask Eli next door how to use the sextant properly.
I will, I will, okay.
Truth be told, I was too embarrassed to let on that I was still having problems with this fine art.
So she sometimes writes we, which includes her cat.
Our course for St.
Thomas, a 900-mile passage that was expected to last about 10 days, led directly into the Bermuda Triangle.

After slowly crossing the Sargasso Sea, she caught trade winds and writes, *My spare time between pumping the bilge was spent trying to figure out where we were by dead reckoning in the occasional sun sights, which more often than not still weren't working out the way they should have.
I kept changing sail and course according to my latest calculations until the estimated afternoon before landfall.*
Sitting in the cockpit, confident that I would be enjoying a cold Coca-Cola in St.
Thomas the next day.
I spied a ship on the horizon and hailed it on the VHF radio just to make sure.
The radio operator's satellite fix notified me that with our present course in position, Veruna would hit land somewhere in the middle of Puerto Rico.
Shocked, not to mention a little bit worried about my dubious talents, I thanked him, signed off, and quickly readjusted our course to the southeast.
So she did make it to St.
Thomas and then on to Puerto Rico.
This was down the east coast, then through the Panama Canal along the west coast of Central America,
and then turned west away from South America toward the Galapagos Islands, where she continues.
On September 11th, my navigation confirmed a monumental occasion.
We had crossed the equator and entered the southern hemisphere.
For the inaugural milestone of the trip, there were presents to open, and I decided to cheer up, throw myself a party, and do it right.
First, I cleaned the boat and then wedged into the cockpit, took a bucket bath.
Drying out in the sun, I noticed that the boat immediately began to smell better.
After the party, in the middle of the night, I woke up, went on deck for a routine horizon check,
and saw a fishing boat in the distance.
I had been trying to hail several boats, and it had seemed that no one kept radio watches.
So it was a great surprise to have this one answer my call.
The world crashed around me when the fix they provided still pinpointed us north of the equator.
My navigation was completely wrong, and we wouldn't cross that line until tomorrow.
Anxiety ridden for the next couple of days, I checked and rechecked the calculations, but couldn't find the error.
Please, God, I prayed, let me find land.
I worried myself literally to tears and dreamed of arriving up a strange river on the wrong island in the Galapagos.
On day 14, after many calculations, minus a couple of fingernails, I convinced myself that I would see land.
I awoke hopeful and turned on the radio direction finder.
Theoretically, we should have been within range, but no signal verified my beliefs.
My eyes burned as I endlessly scouted the horizon for a fishing boat that knew its own position.
Finally, the tension was too much.
I turned Varuna around and headed east, away from supposed land, to avoid passing it accidentally.
Pulling out my Bible, I read a passage from the Psalms and prayed for inspiration.
I was a quivering mess and for good reason.
If we missed the islands of the Galapagos, turning back would be close to impossible.
The currents and winds of the trade route would not allow for the magnitude of such an error.
From there, it was almost 3,000 miles to the next land.
So let's pause aside here to examine these voices.
Do you ever hear them?
I'm such a screw up.
I'm a fraud.
There's something wrong with me.
My mom or dad was right.
I can't do this.
When we sit down on the cushion, we bring the intention to notice what is.
This requires a dedication to seeing the truth and a willingness to see beyond expectation.
Of course, we're messed up.
And of course, we're perfect.
And of course, there is no one to be perfect or messed up.
Maybe it's a little easier to take the next step toward change when we recognize that we're in this mess together and stepping forward together, even alone.
Back to Tanya Avey.
What could be the problem?
The sextant?
The sextant.
I lept to fetch it.
To every problem, there is a solution.
This time, it was the sextant.
I had been using the plastic one that had been aboard my father's boat.
Through the years, the plastic must have warped because the angles I was getting between the sun and the horizon were slightly off.
An unaligned sextant will get you nowhere.
Luckily, in the bottom of one of my lockers lived an excellent aluminum fray burger sextant.
I hadn't wanted to use it because it was heavier and more complicated than the other.
I practiced taking sun sights with it, did all the calculations, and hit our position spot every time.
The treasure was right there all along.
I see this story of the sextant as a metaphor for our practice.
We're not looking for something that isn't already there.
Many Buddhist teachings use a treasure as analogy for enlightenment, a treasure which we already possess, but which we might not perceive.
So here are a few.
Hidden Lamp has the story of the old woman in the Pure Land.
In China and Japan, many millions of Buddhists have been in, and in Japan still are, devotees of the Pure Land doctrine.

According to this doctrine, a Bodhisattva made a great vow, which in time fulfilled itself as the manifestation of the Buddha Amitabha, infinite light, who created a Pure Land paradise in the West for those who would take his name with faith.
From this Pure Land, it was easy to attain final nirvana.
An old lady of this faith was walking along the road when she met a Zen master, who said to her,
*On your way to the Pure Land, eh, granny?*
She nodded.
*Holy Amitabha's there waiting to see you, I expect.* She shook her head.
*No.
Not there?
The Buddhist not in his Pure Land?
And where is he?*
She tapped twice over her heart and went on her way.
The Zen master opened his eyes wide in appreciation and said, You are a real Pure Lander.

In Emela Heller's reflection on this, she mentions that we pilgrims on the path are like the man in the Lotus Sutra, who wanders around the world in poverty while all the time has a priceless jewel sewn into his ragged coat.
As Yunmen told his assembly, within heaven and earth, through space and time, there is a jewel hidden inside the mountain of form.
And that's from the hidden lamp, from the transmission of the lamp.
We have the story where Dai Zhu visited Master Basso in China.
Basso asked, What do you seek?
Enlightenment replied Dai Zhu.
*You have your own treasure house.
Why do you search outside?* Basso asked.
Dai Zhu inquired, *Where is my treasure house?* Basso answered, *What you are asking is your treasure house.* Dai Zhu was delighted.
Ever after he urged his friends, open your own treasure house and use those treasures.
And one more.
Andy Ferguson, Zen's Chinese heritage, has a story of when Juefeng and Yantou were stuck on an inn during a snowstorm while on pilgrimage.
This is an oft quoted story in our circles.

Juefeng said, *Later I asked Deshan, Can a student understand the essence of the ancient teachings?* He struck me and said, *What did you say?* At that moment, it was like the bottom falling out of a bucket of water, which usually means, Aha, he got it.
Yantou said, *Haven't you heard it said that what comes through the front gate isn't the family jewels?
Family jewels not coming through the front gate, they're already in the house.*
So all of that suggesting the treasure is already here.
So is it that easy?
If it was that easy, we would just sit in meditation, look within, and bang, there's the treasure.
Let's go on to something else.
Juefeng's fleeting realization was after decades of practice.
So what obscures our vision of the treasure?
Here's Buddha's teaching on what is obscuring our vision.
It is the five hindrances.
Desire, aversion, dullness, restlessness, and doubt.
We're unable to see the bottom as he compares this process of ours to looking for a clear reflection in water.
Buddha said, *The main impediments to the development of serenity and insight are collectively called the five hindrances.

As we studied before, just as the different impurities of water prevent us from clearly seeing the reflection of our face in a bowl of water, so the five hindrances prevent us from properly understanding our own good and the good of others.
A meditator's initial efforts, therefore, have to be devoted to the task of overcoming the hindrances.
And in the Sangharavasutra, Buddha says, Suppose, Brahmin, there is a bowl of water mixed with red, yellow, blue, or crimson dye.
If a man with good sight were to examine his own facial reflection in it, he would neither know nor see it as it really is.*
So too, Brahmin, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust.
Even those texts that have been recited over a long period do not recur to the mind, let alone those that have not been recited.

Again, Brahmin, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, overwhelmed by ill will, and one does not understand as it really is the escape from a risen ill will, on that occasion one neither knows nor sees as it really is one's own good, or the good of others, or the good of both.
Then even those texts which have been recited over a long period do not recur in the mind, let alone those that have not been recited.
Suppose, Brahmin, there is a bowl of water being heated over a fire, bubbling and boiling.
If a man with good sight were to examine his own facial reflection in it, he would neither know nor see it as it really is.
So too, Brahmin, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will.
Even those texts that have been recited over a long period of time do not recur to the mind, let alone those that have not been recited.

Again, Brahmin, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by dullness and drowsiness, overwhelmed by dullness and drowsiness, and one does not understand as it really is the escape from a risen dullness and drowsiness, on that occasion one neither knows nor sees as it really is one's own good, or the good of others, or the good of both.
Then even those texts that have been recited over a long period do not recur in the mind, let alone those that have not been recited.
Suppose, Brahmin, there is a bowl of water covered over with water plants and algae.
If a man with good sight were to examine his own facial reflection in it, he would neither know nor see it as it really is.
So too, Brahmin, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by dullness and drowsiness.
Even those texts that have been recited over a long period do not recur to the mind, let alone those that have not been recited.
Again, Brahmin, when one dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, overwhelmed, we'll skip a little bit.
So the bowl covered with plants and algae is like restlessness and remorse.
And again, we can't see the good in ourselves or others, and we'll not be able to live the text that we've been practicing.
And finally, the analogy, suppose, Brahmin, there is a bowl of water stirred by the wind, rippling, swirling, churned into wavelets.
You still can't find your own reflection, and that is like when one dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse.
Even those texts that have been recited over a long period of time do not recur to the mind, let alone those that have been recited.
We've studied the five hindrances before, and here's some encouragement for what we're doing there.
We're trying to see that treasure that is already within.
May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
